notes:
I've done the research and organised it verse by verse. Each point has its page URL, and the citation tags show the exact source sentences.

**What I couldn't find, so it's left out:** No Orthodox (oca.org) material, no Lutheran sources, nothing from bibleodyssey.org, and nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers on this chapter. For Methodist and Wesleyan views I only found Benson's and Wesley's notes, quoted inside studylight.org pages. The only Catholic source was a short newadvent.org encyclopedia entry. Vv. 20–22 have almost no comment of their own.

**Tradition labels:** Enduring Word is David Guzik, who is Calvary Chapel. You listed that site under Pentecostal and charismatic, so I've used it there, but he isn't a classic Pentecostal. Coffman is Restoration Movement. Constable and GotQuestions are evangelical and dispensational.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** Guzik says the power of Ezra's confession lay in the depth of heart shown by his weeping and bowing. He sees the people's weeping as being convicted of sin themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- **Grammar:** Guzik cites Yamauchi that the Hebrew grammar suggests Ezra kept throwing himself to the ground. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- **Who gathered:** Utley says that normally only men over thirteen would make up such a gathering. He wonders whether these Jewish women and children had been hurt by the foreign marriages (Mal. 2:10–16). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **Ellicott:** The evil penetrated domestic life, and the punishment, as was already foreseen by "the women bringing the children with them," brought special family distress. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-4.html
- **Charismatic/revival emphasis (Guzik):** He calls this conviction a mark of a powerful move of the Holy Spirit. He supports it with stories from later revivals collected by J. Edwin Orr, and gives general guidelines for confessing sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**v. 2**
- **Who Shecaniah was:** Gill thinks Shecaniah had not married a foreign wife himself, but speaks this way because his nation, his father and several uncles had (v. 26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-2.htm
  - Guzik praises him for standing beside the guilty even though his own family was involved. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
  - Utley identifies him as the son of one of the offenders listed in v. 26. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **What "hope" means: readings differ**
  - Guzik: their brokenness was an emblem of the work of God's Spirit among them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
  - An older note on the same page: The case is sad, but not desperate: the disease threatening, but not incurable. Our ruin may yet be prevented by repentance and reformation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-2.htm
  - Geneva Bible: it means that God would receive them in mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-2.htm
  - Another note says Shecaniah relied upon the promise attached to repentance (e.g. Deuteronomy 30:1-10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-2.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch base the hope on the solemn covenant the people were about to make. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-2.htm
  - Matthew Henry's line about trouble becoming a door of hope: the sin that truly troubles us shall not ruin us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-4.html
- **A critical older voice:** The Expositor's Bible (1887, Adeney) says the hope is for reform, not for excusing the offence. It calls this a grim kind of hope, worthy of the name only on the lips of a fanatic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezra-10.html
- **"Peoples of the land":** Utley says that before the exile this phrase meant the Jewish population. Here it means the people of the Persian province. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **Ethnic or religious?** Bible Hub's study notes say The issue is not ethnic but religious, as these marriages led to the worship of foreign gods. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-2.htm

**v. 3: the most debated verse**
- **Why a covenant:** Utley says they were renewing a covenant they had broken, perhaps out of ignorance of the Torah. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
  - The Pulpit Commentary thinks Shecaniah had in mind the covenant made under Zedekiah to free slaves (Jer. 34:15). https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-3.htm
- **"My lord":** Utley takes it as Ezra, a plural of majesty. He notes the Vulgate reads it as God. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
  - Parker's People's Bible says it should read "the Lord" and does not refer to Ezra. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/ezra/10-44.html
- **"According to the Law": two readings**
  - Barnes takes it to mean a formal bill of divorce, which left the woman free to remarry (Deut. 24:1–2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-3.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary allows either "let the law that forbids these marriages be satisfied" or "let the divorce follow the legal procedure." https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-3.htm
- **Were these real marriages?**
  - One older commentator on the Bible Hub page held that marriages forbidden by God were, properly speaking, no marriages at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-3.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says Shecaniah probably thought them invalid, not just wrong. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-3.htm
  - Another note on the commentary page disagrees: The marriages had been valid, but were now declared sinful. The method of separation was forcible expulsion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-3.htm
- **The children**
  - The Pulpit Commentary cites the maxim that children follow their mother, and adds that older children might already be tainted by idolatry. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-3.htm
  - Guzik cites Yamauchi that mothers normally got custody, and Clarke that the women were surely given support. He notes that Adeney thought this was excessive zeal, but himself concludes it was God's will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
  - Gill (on v. 44) thinks the children may not have been sent away, but kept and raised in the true religion. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/gnt/ezra/10-44.html
  - Benson (Methodist) makes a similar suggestion: Ezra may have softened Shecaniah's proposal, since v. 11 mentions only the wives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-11.html
- **Corporate thinking:** Utley says modern Westerners struggle with the Bible's corporate outlook, and that the faithfulness of the "holy seed" was crucial to God's plan. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **Where Protestant teachers differ on whether this applies today**
  - **Reformed (Ligonier):** The text is narrative, so The community may have erred in these divorces (Ezra 10:6–17). Given Ezra's positive portrayal, however, it seems more likely that the divorces were right. It suggests the wives may have broken laws that applied even to foreigners, so divorce was the nearest thing to obeying the law. Under the new covenant, a believer should not divorce a willing unbelieving spouse (1 Cor. 7:12–16). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/putting-away-the-foreign-wives
  - **Baptist (MacArthur):** He says this is the only time in the Old Testament God tells someone to divorce. He calls it merciful compared with the death penalty of Deut. 7, and says it sets no permanent standard. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/90-231/gods-view-of-divorce-part-1
  - **Dispensational (GotQuestions):** It belonged to an earlier dispensation, and Christians today should not look to this account for justification to divorce a spouse. https://www.gotquestions.org/abandon-foreign-wives-children.html
  - **Constable:** God hates divorce but permitted it here for Israel's distinct calling. His purposes for the church are not the same as His purposes for Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-11.html
  - **Kidner (cited by Guzik):** This was a choice of the lesser of two evils. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- **Modern evangelical scholarship (bible.org):**
  - Some scholars see Deut. 24:1 behind it. Joe Sprinkle treats the wives' idolatry as the "indecent thing" of that law. https://bible.org/seriespage/chapter-6-holiness-ezra-separated-uncleanness-and-seeking-lord
  - Heth and Wenham think Ezra was annulling unlawful unions rather than ending legitimate marriages. Same page.
  - The author notes that the law forbids none of these mixed marriages for Moabites, Ammonites or Egyptians, and that no law or prophet names divorce as the remedy. Same page.
  - The author concludes that the legal question doesn't matter to the story's point: Ezra saw the separation as consistent with the law and part of repentance. Same page.

**v. 4**
- **Ezra's authority:** Clarke notes the decree of Artaxerxes authorised Ezra to do whatever God's law required (Ezra 7:23–28). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-4.html
- **Why Ezra didn't propose it himself:** Guzik suggests Ezra was too distressed, or knew the idea had to come from the community rather than a newcomer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- **"Be strong and act":** Utley links this to God's charge to Joshua and sums it up: "Put feet to your prayers!" https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **Puritan application:** The Biblical Illustrator says there will be no reform till the word of Ezra and the sword of Shechaniah go together. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-4.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik notes that Ezra began with the leaders, expecting them to put things right first. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- Utley says priests, Levites and Israel are the three levels of society. He adds that Ezra wanted their change of heart sealed by an oath. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- Coffman: Ezra very wisely moved at once to have everyone swear to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-4.html

**v. 6**
- Utley calls it a total fast, like those of Moses and Nineveh. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- Guzik says that for Ezra this was like a death in the family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- **Modern dating debate:** Some use Jehohanan son of Eliashib to argue that Ezra came after Nehemiah. Utley says both names are too common to decide it, and cites Kidner. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648

**v. 7**
- Utley says the returnees' territory was small, so everyone could reach Jerusalem. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648

**v. 8**
- **"Forfeit":** Utley says the word is *herem*, property devoted to God, as with Jericho. The person was also shut out of the community. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- Guzik says Ezra was using the civil authority Artaxerxes gave him (Ezra 7:26). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**v. 9**
- **Date and weather:** Utley says the ninth month is Kislev, midwinter, so they trembled from the cold rain as well as from fear. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
  - Constable dates the meeting to late November or early December 458 BC. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/ezra-10.html
- **Revival reading (Guzik):** He sees their willingness to sit in the rain as another sign of the Spirit at work. He compares a street meeting in freezing rain during the 1859 Ulster revival. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**v. 10**
- **"Married" literally:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew is literally "caused to dwell," meaning they had brought these women to live in the holy land. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-10.htm
- **Ethnicity:** Bible Hub's notes say The issue is not ethnicity but idolatry (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-10.htm

**v. 11**
- **"Confession":** Utley says the Hebrew word also means to give praise, so confession was itself an act of worship (Josh. 7:19). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
  - The Pulpit Commentary holds that "make confession" is the true sense here, not the Septuagint's "give praise." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-11.html
- **Why separate:** The Pulpit Commentary says the marriages led to close ties with the wives' relatives, wearing down the wall between Jew and Gentile that the law of Moses set up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-11.html
- **Confession and repentance:** Guzik says confession would be empty without repentance. He cites Spurgeon that repentance lasts as long as faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**v. 12**
- Utley traces the repeated verb "do" through the chapter (vv. 3, 4, 5, 11, 12, 16): faith must turn into action. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- Guzik sees their loud, immediate agreement as further evidence of the Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**vv. 13–14**
- **Investigating each case:** Utley thinks each case had to be examined, because some wives had become converts and were raising their children to worship the LORD while others had not. He also suggests some men had divorced Jewish wives to marry these women (Mal. 2). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
  - The bible.org holiness study counters that nothing in Ezra suggests these men had divorced Jewish wives. https://bible.org/seriespage/chapter-6-holiness-ezra-separated-uncleanness-and-seeking-lord
- **Converted wives:** Another bible.org lesson presumes that a wife who gave up her idols needed to do nothing more. Where she refused, the marriage was ended, presumably with provision made for her and the children. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-10-genuine-repentance-ezra-101-44
- **How it worked:** The Pulpit Commentary describes a standing commission that took each town in turn with its local elders and judges. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-11.html
- Guzik notes they asked only for time; they agreed with the principle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**v. 15: translation dispute**
- **The KJV reading:** The KJV says these four men "were employed about this matter." Gill and another older commentator take it that way: two priests helped by Levites, keeping records and running the process. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-15.htm
- **The modern reading:** Barnes notes that others translate "opposed this," and that The opposition was useless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-15.htm
- Utley takes "opposed," citing the same idiom elsewhere. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **Unknown motives:** A Bible Hub topical entry says the text gives no reasons for their opposition. https://biblehub.com/topical/j/jahzeiah.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Utley counts 110 cases investigated in 75 days. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- Constable says the work took three months and involved 113 men in all, a small fraction of Judah. He adds that about 25% of them were priests or Levites. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/ezra-10.html

**v. 18**
- Utley says even the family of the first high priest, Jeshua, was neither spared nor covered up. He notes that 1 Esdras 9:19 says Jeshua himself was not involved. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **Who was involved:** Barnes lists 4 from the high priest's family and 13 other priests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm

**v. 19**
- **"Pledged":** Utley says it literally means "gave their hand," a gesture sealing an agreement. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- **The guilt offering:** Utley links it to Lev. 5, which covers unintentional sin. It's unclear whether one ram was offered for all or one each. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648

**vv. 20–22**
- Utley says only four priestly families returned (Ezra 2:36–38), and the same four are named here: Jeshua, Immer, Harim and Pashhur. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
- Bible Hub's study notes on v. 44 say even spiritual leaders were caught up in this, and that naming them shows Scripture's accountability and transparency. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-44.htm

---

**Catholic view (whole passage):** The Catholic Encyclopedia retells it as Ezra's first reform. It says the "strange wives" were dismissed after a commission sat for three full months, and offers no moral judgment. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05535a.htm

**1 Esdras parallel:** An ISBE entry on classic.net.bible.org says 1 Esdras 8:91–9:36 covers the same events as Ezra 10. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Esdras,+The+First+Book+Of
- Utley notes that the RSV takes from 1 Esdras 9:36 the reading that the men sent the wives away along with their children. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21648
